q: What does the plus sign in dbt run --select +silver_orders mean?
a: Build that model and everything upstream of it.

q: Why did the class's models end up in DBT_DEV?
a: dbt builds into the schema set in the profile's target, and that was DBT_DEV.

q: What is a dbt test?
a: A query that looks for bad records. If it returns zero rows the test passes; any rows and it fails.

q: Why did setting a status to "banana" still pass the tests at first?
a: Only not_null and unique tests existed, and banana breaks neither. A test can only catch what you defined, so it failed once an accepted_values test was added.

q: Do dbt tests check the schema or the data?
a: The data. They inspect the actual values in the table.

q: Where should dbt tests go?
a: Ideally at the source layer, but it's good practice to test Silver and Gold too, because unexpected things happen.

q: What do data engineering interviewers usually ask about?
a: Your projects' pipelines: the source, ingestion, processing and storage, and which part you had the biggest impact on. Be ready to talk about every project on your CV.

q: What's the difference between a Region and an Availability Zone?
a: A Region is a geographic area like N. Virginia. Each Region has several Availability Zones, which are separate data centers with their own power and networking, so one can fail without taking the others down.

q: How do you choose a Region?
a: By latency to your users, by cost, and by data-residency laws, like EU data having to stay in the EU.

q: If you wanted to grant yourself certain permissions, which service would you use?
a: IAM, by attaching policies to your user, a group you're in, or a role you assume.

q: What's the difference between a user and a role in IAM?
a: A user is a person or app with long-term credentials. A role has no password; a service or user assumes it to get temporary credentials, which is safer for anything running inside AWS.

q: What is the discrete unit in S3?
a: The bucket, which is what you create and configure: Region, permissions, versioning. Inside it, data is stored as objects, each identified by a key.

q: Why put Bronze, Silver and Gold in separate buckets?
a: Permissions and lifecycle rules are simpler and safer at the bucket level, a mistake in one layer can't wipe out another, and costs can be tracked per layer.

q: What is S3 Glacier?
a: A set of cheaper S3 storage tiers for long-term data you rarely read. Retrieval is slower and costs extra.

q: What is EBS?
a: Persistent block storage attached to an EC2 instance, like its hard drive. It's how you keep things on an instance across stops and starts.

q: What's the difference between IAM and a VPC?
a: IAM controls who can perform which actions. A VPC controls which network traffic can reach a resource at all.

q: What's the difference between Hadoop and EMR?
a: Hadoop is the open-source software. EMR is AWS's managed service that runs Hadoop and Spark on EC2 for you, usually with S3 instead of HDFS so the cluster can be shut down.

q: What does serverless mean?
a: There are still servers, but you never manage them. The provider supplies compute when your work runs, and you pay only for that time.

q: What is EventBridge?
a: An event bus that fires actions when things happen in AWS, like starting a Glue job when a file arrives in S3. It can also run things on a schedule.

q: What is AWS Glue?
a: Serverless Spark with its own UI and its own DynamicFrame style of programming, plus the Data Catalog. Instead of nodes, you size it in DPUs.

q: What is a DPU and how does Glue charge?
a: A DPU is a serverless unit of compute, 4 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory. Glue bills DPU-hours per second while the job runs, so more data costs more indirectly through longer runs or more DPUs.

q: When do you use EMR versus Glue?
a: EMR when the compute is busy all the time and you want control. Glue when data arrives occasionally and you don't want to pay for idle time in between.

q: How do you ingest data into Redshift?
a: With the COPY command, which loads files from S3 in parallel across all the slices. Split the data into multiple files for speed.

q: How did Redshift change with Serverless?
a: Provisioned clusters took about 30 minutes to set up and billed for uptime. Serverless is ready almost immediately and bills for compute only while queries run, plus storage.

q: What is MPP?
a: Massively parallel processing: one query is split across many nodes that each work on their own data at the same time, and the results are combined. Moving data between nodes is the slow part.

q: What's the difference between RDS and Redshift?
a: RDS is a row-based OLTP database for an application's many small reads and writes, and it's usually a pipeline source. Redshift is a columnar OLAP warehouse for big analytical queries, usually the destination.

q: What is Athena?
a: A serverless SQL query engine that queries files in S3 directly using schema on read. It stores no data; the table schemas come from the Glue Data Catalog.

q: What's the difference between the Glue Crawler and the Glue Data Catalog?
a: The crawler scans files and figures out the schema in the moment, but stores nothing. The Data Catalog stores the schema long term so Athena, Glue and EMR can use it.

q: What is DynamoDB?
a: A serverless NoSQL key-value and document database. Items are looked up by partition key, optionally with a sort key, with very fast single-digit-millisecond reads at any scale.

q: Describe a modern serverless lakehouse pipeline on AWS.
a: Data lands in a Bronze S3 bucket, Glue cleans it into Silver and then builds Gold, stored in S3 or Redshift Serverless. Athena handles ad-hoc queries, Redshift serves dashboards, and RDS or DynamoDB serve applications.

q: Describe Evan's batch pipeline on AWS from start to finish.
a: Raw data lands in S3, a Spark job on EMR Serverless cleans and transforms it, the results are loaded into Redshift Serverless as a warehouse, and a Streamlit app running in a container on ECS with Fargate shows dashboards.

q: Why does the Citi Bike pipeline need to exist at all?
a: The GBFS feed only shows the current moment. If you want history, like which stations run empty at rush hour, you have to save a snapshot every few minutes yourself.

q: What are the three GBFS feeds we used and how are they different?
a: gbfs.json is the discovery file listing the other feeds' URLs, station_information has slow-changing details like name and capacity, and station_status has the live counts of bikes and docks available.

q: Why is Bronze data stored exactly as the API returned it?
a: So you can always reprocess. If the Silver logic has a bug, you fix the script and rerun it on the untouched raw files.

q: Why are the Bronze hour folders in UTC?
a: So everyone in the pipeline agrees on one time zone. A file saved at 2:28 PM New York time lands in hour 18.

q: What's the difference between a trust policy and a permissions policy?
a: The trust policy says who is allowed to assume the role, like the Lambda service. The permissions policy says what the role can do once assumed, like PutObject on the Bronze prefix.

q: Why can't the EventBridge Scheduler just use the Lambda's role?
a: That role only trusts lambda.amazonaws.com. The scheduler is a different service, so it needs its own role that trusts scheduler.amazonaws.com and allows lambda:InvokeFunction.

q: The Lambda test works but nothing arrives on schedule. What do you check?
a: That the scheduler role has lambda:InvokeFunction and trusts the scheduler service, and that the schedule's start time has arrived and end time hasn't passed.

q: Inside a Lambda, where do the AWS credentials come from?
a: From the function's IAM role. You just call boto3.client("s3") with no profile or keys.

q: What's the difference between an EMR Serverless application and a job run?
a: The application is the reusable Spark environment you create once. A job run is a single execution of your script on it.

q: Why does the Spark read need the multiLine option?
a: Each Bronze file is one JSON document spread over many lines, and Spark's default expects one JSON object per line.

q: What does explode do in the Bronze to Silver job?
a: It turns one row per file, which holds a list of about 2,500 stations, into one row per station.

q: Why did the first EMR job run fail, and what's the lesson?
a: The script referenced num_vehicles_available, a field from a newer GBFS version. The real feed uses num_bikes_available. The lesson is to always validate a transform against a real data sample.

q: Does Fargate cost nothing when idle?
a: No. Fargate bills for every second a task runs. It only costs nothing if you stop the task, which a website usually can't do.

q: Does Block Public Access need to be turned off for Lambda or EMR to use the bucket?
a: No. Those services reach the bucket through IAM, which works with Block Public Access on. Leave it on.

q: How do you get AWS CLI access as an IAM user?
a: Click your username, go to Security credentials, create an access key for the CLI and download the CSV, then run aws configure with the key ID, secret, region us-east-2 and JSON output, and test with aws s3 ls.

q: Why did Evan keep getting "the security token included in the request is invalid"?
a: His keys are stored under a named profile, so commands without --profile company used other keys. It's an authentication problem, not a permissions problem.

q: What is incremental loading?
a: Regularly bringing only new data into a system in small batches, like every five minutes. It isn't streaming, which is continuous.

q: Why use Glue instead of EMR, according to Evan?
a: EMR is closer to the original Hadoop and Spark technology and runs plain Spark. Glue can also run plain Spark but has its own API and data structures, like the DynamicFrame, so you choose Glue when you want that API.

q: Why couldn't the Glue job reuse the EMR role?
a: A role's trust policy names which service can assume it. The EMR role trusts EMR Serverless, so Glue needs a role that trusts glue.amazonaws.com.

q: Evan's create-job succeeded on the CLI but the console showed nothing. Why?
a: The CLI's default region was us-east-1 while the console was on us-east-2.

q: What is an implicit deny?
a: IAM denies everything by default. If no statement allows an action on that exact resource, it's denied even without a Deny statement, like when an object ARN is missing the /* at the end.

q: Why did the Glue job need s3:DeleteObject?
a: It wrote in overwrite mode, which deletes existing files first. Switching to append only adds files.

q: What is a DPU?
a: A Data Processing Unit, Glue's compute unit: 4 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory. It measures allocated compute, not speed.

q: What's the difference between a Redshift Serverless namespace and workgroup?
a: The namespace is the storage side: databases, tables, users and IAM roles. The workgroup is the compute side: RPUs, network settings and the endpoint you connect to.

q: What is ingress versus egress?
a: Ingress is traffic coming into a system; egress is traffic going out.

q: Why did creating the Glue connection to Redshift fail for an administrator?
a: Using a password made Glue try to create a Secrets Manager secret, which was denied, and the workgroup didn't have an admin password set in the first place.

q: What's a DynamicFrame?
a: Glue's version of a DataFrame that doesn't require a strict schema, designed for messy or nested JSON. You convert with DynamicFrame.fromDF and toDF.

q: What does redshift_tmp_dir do in a Glue write to Redshift?
a: Glue stages the data as files in S3 there, and Redshift bulk-loads them with COPY.

q: What error ended the class, and what kind of problem was it?
a: "Could not find S3 endpoint or NAT gateway for subnet." A networking problem: the job ran in Redshift's private subnet with no route to S3.

q: Why are Glue and Redshift in the same VPC in Evan's diagram, while S3 is outside?
a: Services that talk to each other should share a private network so traffic stays local and secure. S3 is a globally available object store designed for availability, so it normally isn't inside your VPC.

q: What caused "Could not find S3 endpoint or NAT gateway for subnet" and how is it fixed?
a: The Glue connection made the job run inside Redshift's private subnet, which had no route to S3. You fix it by adding an S3 gateway endpoint to that subnet's route table.

q: What's the difference between an Internet Gateway and a NAT Gateway?
a: An Internet Gateway gives public resources two-way internet access. A NAT Gateway lets private resources make outbound connections without being reachable from outside, and it costs money.

q: What's the difference between a gateway endpoint and an interface endpoint?
a: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, work through the route table and are free. Interface endpoints cover most other services, create a network interface in your subnet and are billed.

q: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
a: Authentication checks who you are, like credentials or tokens. Authorization decides what you're allowed to do once you're in, like IAM policies.

q: Why did students need sqlworkbench permissions when they already had Redshift Serverless access?
a: Redshift Query editor v2 is a separate service with its own IAM prefix, sqlworkbench, so redshift-serverless permissions don't cover it.

q: What is AWS Secrets Manager?
a: A service that stores credentials like database passwords encrypted in one place, so services read them at runtime instead of having them in code. It supports rotation and audit logging.

q: You can open the query editor but get "permission denied for relation." What's going on?
a: IAM got you in, but inside the database your user hasn't been granted access to that table. The table's owner has to run a GRANT.

q: What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
a: WHERE filters individual rows before any aggregation. HAVING filters groups after a GROUP BY, so it can use aggregates like COUNT.

q: What does QUALIFY do?
a: It filters on the result of a window function, the way WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups. For example, keeping only rows where ROW_NUMBER equals one.

q: What's the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
a: DELETE removes specific rows one by one and can use a WHERE. TRUNCATE quickly removes all rows but keeps the table. DROP removes the table itself.

q: Why create dimension tables before the fact table?
a: The fact table references the dimensions through foreign keys, so the dimensions need to exist and be populated first.

q: Why did dim_station have 97 rows but the fact table 100?
a: Different grains. The dimension is one row per station; the fact is one row per station per snapshot, and three stations had two snapshots.

q: Name the three validation checks Evan ran and why.
a: Row counts per table, orphaned facts with a left join where the dimension key is null, and duplicate facts with group by having count greater than one. They make sure the Gold data is correct before analysis, since Redshift doesn't enforce keys.

q: Why is a star schema used for analytics?
a: It's the gold standard for analytical data. Measurements sit in a central fact table at a declared grain, descriptions sit in dimension tables, so descriptions aren't repeated, business logic is defined once, and every question is a simple fact-plus-joins query.

q: What does CASE WHEN do and how did Evan use it?
a: It's SQL's if-statement. He used SUM of CASE WHEN is_empty THEN 1 ELSE 0 END to count how often each station was empty, then turned it into a percentage.

q: What does NULLIF do in a percentage calculation?
a: NULLIF of the count and zero returns null when the count is zero, so dividing gives null instead of a division-by-zero error.

q: Evan's hourly query showed hours 18 to 20. What do they mean?
a: The timestamps are UTC, so those are 2 to 4 PM New York time, not evening hours.

q: What's the closest SQL equivalent to the factory design pattern?
a: A stored procedure: saved, named SQL logic you call instead of rewriting the same queries.

q: What is this weekend's homework?
a: Rebuild the full pipeline on your side: Lambda ingestion into S3, EMR or Glue from Bronze to Silver, Silver to Gold in Redshift as a star schema, and analytical queries, while letting the ingestion run over the weekend to collect more data.

q: What three disciplines go into designing a warehouse beyond dimensional modeling?
a: Logical data architecture, which is how entities and business meaning are organized; physical database design, which is how data is stored for performance; and enterprise data architecture, which sets the boundaries between ingestion, transformation and consumption.

q: How is Gold different from Silver, and Serving different from Gold?
a: Gold changes the shape, into a star schema with dimensions stored once. Serving changes the grain, with aggregates at the level the business asks about, like one row per station per day.

q: What is a conformed dimension?
a: A dimension shared across fact tables where the meaning matches, like one date or station dimension used by both trips and snapshots.

q: What is Kinesis Data Streams?
a: A serverless equivalent of Kafka. Producers write to a stream, consumers read from it, and it scales with shards instead of brokers and partitions.

q: What's the difference between Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose?
a: Data Streams holds the messages for your own consumer code to process. Firehose is the consumer: you point it at a destination like S3 or Redshift and it delivers the data without you writing a consumer.

q: What's the difference between MSK and Kinesis?
a: MSK is real Apache Kafka managed by AWS, so you use standard Kafka code and get more control. Kinesis is AWS's own Kafka-like service with its own SDK calls and less control, but it's serverless with minimal setup.

q: What's a shard?
a: Kinesis's unit of capacity, like a Kafka partition. Each shard handles about 1 MB per second or 1,000 records per second of writes.

q: What does the partition key do in a Kinesis put_record call?
a: It's hashed to choose the shard, so all records with the same key, like one station, go to the same shard and stay in order.

q: When would you use the Kinesis Producer Library instead of the SDK?
a: For very high volumes of small records, like 100,000 transactions a second. KPL aggregates, batches and retries records instead of making one API call per record.

q: What does the Kinesis Client Library do?
a: It helps you build your own consumers by handling shard assignment, load balancing across workers, checkpointing and recovery, coordinated through DynamoDB lease tables.

q: What are the stream processing options on AWS?
a: Kinesis Firehose, Spark Structured Streaming on EMR, Glue Streaming, Managed Flink, and Lambda, which is only good in rare cases like demos.

q: Why is Lambda rarely a good streaming consumer?
a: It's not distributed, has a 15-minute limit and keeps no state between invocations. It's fine for demos and light workloads, but not production.

q: Why would you choose Managed Flink for fraud detection?
a: Flink processes each message individually with low latency and keeps per-customer state, which fraud detection needs. Spark Structured Streaming works in micro-batches.

q: What is RAG?
a: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. A pipeline retrieves the most relevant pieces of your own data and adds them to the LLM's prompt, so it can answer questions about data it was never trained on.

q: How is RAG different from a vector database?
a: RAG is the pipeline. A vector database is a kind of storage that holds embeddings and finds the most similar ones, and it's usually one component inside a RAG pipeline.

q: Does RAG retrain the model?
a: No. The retrieved text is added to the prompt at question time. The model's weights don't change.

q: Why is Glue not interchangeable with plain Spark?
a: Glue is serverless and has its own DynamicFrame, built for messy JSON where rows don't all have the same columns. It can run Spark code, but it's a distinct service.

q: The Glue streaming job log says "retrying micro batch processing". What does that mean?
a: A batch is failing. A healthy streaming job doesn't retry, so look for the real error underneath.

q: How do you check that a Kinesis producer is actually sending data?
a: Get a shard iterator, call get-records and decode the data from Base64. If you see valid JSON, the producer and stream are fine and the problem is downstream.

q: An error says assumed-role something is not authorized. Who fixes it?
a: You can. It's the policy on your IAM role, so add the missing permission there. If it says your user is not authorized, that's group permissions and you need an admin.

q: What should you shut down after a streaming demo?
a: The Glue streaming job, because it bills per DPU-hour until stopped. Also check anything that bills per hour, like a provisioned Kinesis stream or an RDS instance.

q: What is Terraform?
a: An Infrastructure as Code tool from HashiCorp. You describe cloud resources in code files, and Terraform creates, changes and deletes them to match.

q: Why use Terraform instead of clicking through the console?
a: Console work can't be repeated and leaves no record. A Terraform file is repeatable and is the single place that says exactly what infrastructure exists and how it connects.

q: What is HCL?
a: HashiCorp Configuration Language, the declarative language Terraform files are written in. You describe what should exist, and Terraform figures out how to get there.

q: What's the difference between a data block and a resource block?
a: A data block looks up something that already exists, like the latest Amazon Linux image, without changing it. A resource block is something Terraform creates and manages, like an EC2 instance.

q: Walk through the Terraform workflow.
a: terraform init downloads the provider plugins. terraform plan shows what will change without changing anything. terraform apply makes the changes after you confirm. terraform destroy deletes everything the configuration created.

q: What should you look for in a Terraform plan?
a: Green plus signs mean resources will be created. Red minus signs mean something will be destroyed, so read those carefully before typing yes.

q: How does Terraform get AWS credentials?
a: The same way the AWS CLI does, from aws configure or a named profile. Keys never go in the Terraform file.

q: What is orchestration?
a: Managing and automating what your resources do: which steps run, in what order, on what schedule, and what happens when one fails. The orchestrator tells services like Glue and Lambda when to work but doesn't do the data work itself.

q: What's the most well-known orchestrator?
a: Apache Airflow, which defines workflows as Python DAGs. AWS offers it managed as MWAA, and Step Functions is AWS's own serverless orchestrator.

q: Is Kubernetes an orchestrator in the same sense?
a: It orchestrates containers, keeping them running and scaled, but it isn't a pipeline scheduler like Airflow or Step Functions.

q: What does the cron expression 0 5 * * 1 mean?
a: At minute 0 of hour 5 on any day of the month, any month, on Monday. So 5 AM every Monday.

q: What does an orchestrator add on top of cron?
a: Cron only decides when something runs. An orchestrator adds dependencies between steps, retries, failure handling and one place to see what happened.

q: What is AWS Step Functions?
a: AWS's serverless workflow orchestrator. You define a state machine of steps, like run a Glue job then a Lambda, with retries and branches, and AWS runs it and tracks each step.

q: What's the difference between Standard and Express workflows?
a: Standard workflows can run up to a year with exactly-once steps and are priced per state transition. Express workflows are short, under five minutes, for high volume, priced per request and duration.

q: What does serverless mean for an application?
a: You don't manage any servers. AWS provisions and scales them, and you pay for what you use, often close to nothing when idle, within service limits like Lambda's 15 minutes.

q: What's the difference between a full refresh and an incremental pipeline?
a: A full refresh reprocesses all the data every run. An incremental pipeline only processes what's new since the last successful run, using a batch window and a checkpoint, so it's cheaper and faster.

q: What is idempotency and why does an incremental pipeline need it?
a: Running something once or many times gives the same result. Batches get retried after failures, so loads must not create duplicates when a batch runs twice.

q: How did the class make loads idempotent?
a: Each batch landed in a landing table tagged with a batch ID, then a MERGE moved it into the canonical table, inserting only new rows and updating or skipping existing ones.

q: What is a stored procedure?
a: A named block of SQL stored inside the database, like a function. You run it with CALL, which makes it easy for an orchestrator to trigger the whole merge with one statement.

q: What is a checkpoint, and when should it advance?
a: The record of the last batch that completed, so the next run knows where to start. It should only advance after the load and validations succeed, so a failed run retries the same window.

q: Why did Evan keep the checkpoint in Redshift instead of DynamoDB?
a: DynamoDB is valid but adds another service with its own permissions and cost. Redshift was already in the pipeline, so it was the simpler choice.

q: Why run the whole merge in one transaction?
a: So Gold is never half-updated. Either the whole batch is applied to the canonical table and every Gold table, or none of it is.

q: What does terraform import do?
a: It links an existing AWS resource to a block in your Terraform code, adding it to Terraform's state, so Terraform can manage infrastructure that was originally built by hand.

q: After an import, what should terraform plan say?
a: No changes. That means the code matches what really exists.

q: Your plan wants to add resources you know already exist. What do you do?
a: Stop and don't apply. You're probably in a folder without the state file, so Terraform thinks nothing exists and would create duplicates.

q: Why did Step Functions fail with permission denied even though the IAM role was right?
a: There are two layers. IAM let the role call the Redshift Data API, but inside Redshift the role's database user had no GRANTs on the tables, so the SQL failed.

q: What does Redrive do in Step Functions?
a: It restarts a failed execution from the failed step, keeping the results of the steps that already succeeded, so the Glue jobs didn't run again.

q: Why schedule the pipeline every 30 minutes instead of every 5?
a: Each run starts two Glue jobs, and every Glue run has startup time and a minimum billed duration. Every 5 minutes would cost far more for little gain.

q: Why create the schedule disabled first?
a: It's a safe rollout. You verify the schedule exists with the right settings, then enable it in a separate, small change.

q: Why does each batch window start two hours before the checkpoint?
a: To pick up files that arrived late. The MERGE removes duplicates, so the overlap is harmless.

q: Why use an inclusive start and exclusive end for the window?
a: So back-to-back windows never count the same file twice or skip one at the boundary.

q: Why turn off Glue job bookmarks?
a: The Redshift checkpoint already tracks what's been processed. Two trackers would conflict.

q: Why does the dashboard read live data from the GBFS API and history from Redshift?
a: Redshift is only as fresh as the last 30-minute batch, so it can't power a live map. The API gives fresh data, and Redshift gives the history.

q: How do you pause the dashboard overnight without risking the pipeline?
a: Stop the EC2 instance with the CLI instead of terraform destroy, which could touch the pipeline resources in the same state. The public IP changes when it restarts.

q: What are the trade-offs of local AI versus hosted AI?
a: Local AI costs only electricity per request and keeps data on your network, but needs expensive hardware and runs smaller, weaker models. Hosted AI like Bedrock charges per token but gives you the strongest models with no hardware.

q: What is a system prompt?
a: Instructions the developer sends with every request that set the model's role, rules and output format, like "you are a Redshift SQL expert, use only this schema, return one read-only query."

q: Why does everything the model needs have to be in the prompt?
a: The model has no memory. It starts blank on every request, so the role, the schema and the rules all have to be sent each time.

q: In the RAG demo, why were the first answers vague?
a: Retrieval was poor, pulling table-of-contents pages. Fixing the retriever, chunking and embeddings, and telling the model to use only the provided context, fixed the answers.

q: What's the difference between RAG with an in-memory index and a vector database?
a: An in-memory index has to be rebuilt every run. A vector database stores the embeddings persistently so they can be searched again without rebuilding.

q: What is Amazon Bedrock?
a: AWS's managed service for calling foundation models from many providers through one API. You don't host the model; you call bedrock-runtime and pay per token.

q: Why use Nova Micro for the chatbot?
a: It's the cheapest model that was good enough for a narrow job like writing SQL, which keeps cost very low. Nova Lite was the fallback if quality wasn't enough.

q: Walk through the text-to-SQL chatbot.
a: The user asks a question in English. Bedrock turns it plus the schema into one read-only SQL query. A person reviews it and clicks to run it on Redshift. Then Bedrock explains the returned rows in plain language.

q: Why have a human approve the SQL before running it?
a: So the AI can't run whatever it wants, like an expensive or wrong query that costs money or causes problems.

q: Why did terraform plan want to recreate the EC2 instance?
a: The AMI was looked up with most_recent, so a newer image made Terraform think the instance had to be replaced. Pinning the AMI ID stops that.

q: How should application code be deployed if Terraform only manages infrastructure?
a: Copy the files to S3, then use SSM Run Command to have the instance pull them and restart its service. You shouldn't rebuild the instance for a Python change.

q: Why did the chatbot return the same station many times?
a: The fact table has one row per station per snapshot, and the SQL ranked raw snapshot rows. The fix was adding grain rules so rankings return one row per station.

q: Why shouldn't you use DISTINCT to fix duplicate rows?
a: It hides the real problem, a bad join or wrong grain, instead of fixing it.

q: How do you filter on a window function in Redshift?
a: Use QUALIFY, or compute it in a CTE and filter on its alias in the outer query. WHERE and HAVING can't filter window functions.

q: The model used a latitude column that doesn't exist. How do you guard against that?
a: Make the prompt require checking every needed column against the schema first, and return INSUFFICIENT_SCHEMA instead of SQL if something is missing.

q: What part of AI does a data engineer usually handle?
a: The deployment side: taking a model someone else built, calling its API, and passing data through prompts. Building and training models belongs to researchers and data scientists.

q: How is the streaming ingestion Lambda different from the batch one?
a: The batch Lambda saved the whole feed as one JSON file in S3. The streaming one splits it into one record per station and publishes them to a Kinesis stream for real-time consumers.

q: Why use the station ID as the partition key?
a: Kinesis hashes the key to choose a shard, so every update for one station lands on the same shard and stays in order.

q: Why does the code send records in chunks of 500?
a: put_records accepts at most 500 records per call, so about 2,500 stations take six calls.

q: What's a partial failure in put_records, and how do you handle it?
a: The call succeeds but some records are rejected, usually from throttling, without raising an error. You check each record's error code and retry only the failed ones, because resending everything would create duplicates.

q: What is exponential backoff?
a: Waiting longer after each failed attempt, like 1, 2, 4 and then 8 seconds, so a throttled shard has time to recover.

q: Why raise an error after five failed attempts?
a: So Lambda marks the run as failed and it shows up in CloudWatch, instead of silently losing data.

q: What is a service-linked role?
a: A role that AWS owns for one specific service. Its trust and permissions are fixed and can't be edited, and creating one needs the iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole permission.

q: Why couldn't the API Destinations service-linked role run the scheduler?
a: It only trusts the EventBridge API Destinations service and only reads Secrets Manager. EventBridge Scheduler needs a normal role that trusts scheduler.amazonaws.com and allows lambda:InvokeFunction.

q: How do you safely pause a cloud pipeline for the weekend?
a: Disable the schedules rather than delete them, confirm nothing is still running, check what any other rules launch, then stop compute like EC2 instances. Disabling a schedule doesn't stop work that's already running.

q: Why does aws scheduler update-schedule with only the state fail?
a: Update replaces the whole schedule. If you leave out the target and role, it fails or overwrites them. You read the schedule, copy its fields, change only the state, and write it back.

q: Why skip schedules that were already disabled?
a: So when you re-enable on Monday, you only turn back on what was running before, not something that was off on purpose.

q: Why check the account ID before running a shutdown script?
a: To make sure you're in the right AWS account and profile, so you don't change someone else's resources.

q: What's the difference between Azure Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2?
a: ADLS Gen2 is Blob Storage with a hierarchical namespace turned on. That gives real directories, atomic directory renames and folder-level ACLs, so it's the storage you use for a data lake.

q: What is a hierarchical namespace?
a: Real directories in object storage. A folder is an actual object in the file system, so renaming or deleting it is one metadata operation instead of copying or deleting every file under it.

q: Why does atomic rename matter for Spark?
a: Spark commits its output by writing to a temporary folder and renaming it to the final folder. On flat storage that's thousands of copies and deletes and not atomic, so a crash can leave a half-moved result.

q: How do you create an ADLS Gen2 account?
a: Create a general-purpose v2 storage account with hierarchical namespace enabled, using `--kind StorageV2 --hns true` in the CLI or the checkbox on the Advanced tab in the portal.

q: Should you write "Azure Blob Storage" on your profile?
a: No. Always say ADLS Gen2. Saying Blob Storage makes it sound like you didn't use a real data lake.

q: What is the ADLS Gen2 path format for Spark?
a: abfss, colon slash slash, container at storage account dot dfs dot core dot windows dot net, then the path. The extra s means TLS, and it uses the dfs endpoint, not blob.

q: What is Microsoft Entra ID?
a: Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure Active Directory. It holds users, groups, service principals and managed identities, and handles sign-in and MFA.

q: What's the difference between Entra ID and Azure RBAC?
a: Entra ID authenticates who you are. RBAC authorizes what you can do: a role assignment gives a principal a role at a scope, like Contributor on a subscription.

q: What's the difference between a tenant and a subscription?
a: The tenant is the organization's Entra ID directory with all its users. A subscription is a billing and access container inside the tenant that holds resource groups and resources. A tenant can have many subscriptions.

q: What is a resource group?
a: A management and lifecycle container for related resources. You can set permissions on it, see its costs, and delete it to delete everything inside. It's not a network like a VPC; Azure's VPC is a VNet.

q: What is a managed identity?
a: An Entra ID identity that Azure creates for a resource, like a data factory or VM, with credentials Azure manages. Your code never stores a password or key.

q: What do Kinesis, EC2, Step Functions and Redshift map to in Azure?
a: Event Hubs, Virtual Machines, Azure Data Factory and Synapse Analytics.

q: What is Azure Event Hubs?
a: A managed event streaming service, basically Kafka in the cloud. A namespace is like a Kafka cluster and an event hub is like a topic, and Kafka clients can connect to it directly.

q: What is Azure Data Factory?
a: Azure's orchestration tool that also does basic low-code ETL with a drag-and-drop pipeline canvas. It's used for the jobs you'd do with Step Functions or Airflow on AWS.

q: What is Delta Lake?
a: An open-source table format and storage layer created by Databricks. Data stays in your own cloud storage as Parquet files plus a _delta_log transaction log, which adds ACID transactions and time travel.

q: What are the three open table formats?
a: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi. Delta is native to Databricks, Iceberg is the vendor-neutral one used by Snowflake, AWS and BigQuery, and Hudi is rarely asked about.

q: What does Unity Catalog do?
a: It's the governance layer for Databricks. One metastore per region is shared by many workspaces, with central permissions, auditing and lineage on catalogs, schemas and tables.

q: Does Unity Catalog let workspaces share clusters?
a: No. Compute still belongs to one workspace. What's shared is the metastore, so every attached workspace sees the same tables and permissions without copying data.

q: What are dev, UAT and prod?
a: Separate environments. Dev is where engineers build, UAT is User Acceptance Testing where the combined work is tested before release, and prod runs the live business.

q: What is Photon?
a: Databricks' vectorized query engine written in C++. It speeds up SQL and DataFrame operations like scans, joins and aggregations, and falls back to normal Spark for anything it doesn't support.

q: Do you need to create a SparkSession in a Databricks notebook?
a: No. The `spark` variable is already defined in every Databricks notebook.

q: Can you use serverless compute with Unity Catalog?
a: Yes. In fact serverless compute requires Unity Catalog.

q: What is Microsoft Fabric?
a: Microsoft's SaaS all-in-one analytics platform built on OneLake. It packages Data Factory, Spark, a warehouse, real-time analytics and Power BI with Copilot. It doesn't include Databricks.

q: Databricks or Snowflake, what's the difference?
a: Databricks started as a Spark lakehouse platform: more control, Python and SQL, your own storage. Snowflake started as a cloud SQL warehouse: simpler, with less control and managed storage.

q: What does AuthorizationFailed mean in Azure?
a: Your identity has no role that allows the action. The message names the object ID, the action and the scope, which is what an admin needs to grant a role like Contributor.

q: What should a final-project presentation cover?
a: A high-concept business question for non-technical management, then the pipeline: ingestion, processing, Bronze/Silver/Gold storage and the analytics that answer the question, using your own data source.

q: What is a Copy activity in Azure Data Factory?
a: The most basic ADF activity. It copies data from a source dataset to a sink dataset, and can convert formats, but it doesn't do real transformations.

q: What's the difference between a linked service and a dataset?
a: A linked service is the connection and authentication to a system, like a database connection. A dataset points to specific data inside it, like a folder, file and format, similar to a table name over that connection.

q: What is an integration runtime?
a: The compute that runs ADF activities and actually moves the data. The Azure IR is managed in the cloud, a self-hosted IR reaches on-prem or private networks, and the Azure-SSIS IR runs SSIS packages.

q: What are the three kinds of ADF activities?
a: Data movement, like Copy; data transformation, like Data Flow, a Databricks notebook or a stored procedure; and control flow, like ForEach, If Condition and Wait.

q: When would you use DMS instead of ADF?
a: For migrating whole databases with little or no transformation, including ongoing change replication. ADF is for pipelines and moderate copies, and AzCopy or Data Box are for bulk files.

q: Why use a managed identity for ADF to reach ADLS?
a: Azure manages the identity's credentials, so no keys or passwords are stored anywhere. You just grant it an RBAC role like Storage Blob Data Contributor on the storage account.

q: Why did the ADLS connection still fail right after granting the role?
a: Azure role assignments take a few minutes to propagate. After waiting, with no other change, the test passed.

q: What's the difference between the control plane and the data plane?
a: The control plane is managing the resource itself, like creating or configuring a storage account, with roles like Contributor. The data plane is reading and writing the files inside, which needs a Storage Blob Data role.

q: What's the most common S3 policy mistake?
a: Putting object actions on the bucket ARN. ListBucket and GetBucketLocation go on the bucket ARN, but GetObject needs the bucket ARN with slash star for the objects.

q: Why use a Binary dataset for the raw copy?
a: Binary copies the bytes as-is without parsing them. That's the right choice for a raw Bronze copy and the fastest option.

q: Why go through all the ADF setup just to copy files?
a: Once it's set up, the pipeline is re-runnable and schedulable with a trigger, and it's often how the company wants it done.

q: How does Databricks read ADLS under Unity Catalog?
a: An Access Connector owns a managed identity, which gets a Storage Blob Data role on the storage account. A storage credential records it, an external location pairs it with an abfss path, and an external volume or tables sit on that location.

q: What's the difference between an external and a managed volume?
a: An external volume governs files that stay in your own ADLS path. A managed volume keeps the files in Unity Catalog's managed storage, so there's no storage permission setup.

q: What does explode do?
a: It turns each element of an array column into its own row. Then select with struct dot star turns the struct's fields into top-level columns.

q: Why use multiLine when reading the Citi Bike JSON?
a: Each file is one JSON document spread over many lines, not one JSON object per line, which is what Spark expects by default.

q: What does overwriteSchema do?
a: It allows a write to change the table's columns or types. Without it, Delta's schema enforcement rejects a write that doesn't match the existing schema.

q: What is a long in Spark?
a: A 64-bit integer, BIGINT. It's not a string. It's the safe type for epoch timestamps.

q: Which duplicate does dropDuplicates keep?
a: It keeps one row per unique combination of the listed columns, but which one survives isn't guaranteed. If it matters, use a window with row_number.

q: How do you keep the latest row per key?
a: Use row_number over a window partitioned by the key and ordered by timestamp descending, then keep rows where it equals one.

q: Why did Gold keep only one snapshot per station per hour?
a: A station can report several times in an hour. Summing all of them would count the same bikes several times, so one snapshot per station per hour gives a true point-in-time total.

q: What goes in Bronze, Silver and Gold?
a: Bronze is raw data plus load metadata, Silver is cleaned, typed and deduplicated data, and Gold is business-level aggregates for analytics.

q: Why does DESCRIBE HISTORY say CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE AS SELECT?
a: An overwrite saveAsTable is logically the same as a CTAS replace. It's the same logic a SQL ELT tool like dbt runs, and every write adds a version for time travel.

q: What does Delta add over plain Parquet?
a: ACID transactions, schema enforcement, a transaction log with version history for time travel, and MERGE, UPDATE and DELETE.

q: Is Azure Databricks different from Databricks on AWS?
a: The notebook and Spark code are the same. Only the cloud integration and authorization setup differ.

q: What's the difference between Spark and Databricks?
a: Spark is the open-source distributed processing engine. Databricks is a managed platform built around it by Spark's creators, adding notebooks, serverless compute, Delta Lake, Unity Catalog, jobs and Photon.

q: How big should a final-project dataset be?
a: Real data, ideally a few gigabytes. Around 5 GB is good for a live demo: big enough to make you think about size, small enough to run in minutes.

q: What is Elasticsearch?
a: A search engine combined with a NoSQL database, built on Apache Lucene. It stores JSON documents and searches them like a search engine, ranked by relevance, instead of with exact SQL queries.

q: Why is Elasticsearch fast at full-text search?
a: Lucene builds an inverted index, a lookup from every word to the documents that contain it, like the index at the back of a book.

q: Why does eBay use Elasticsearch but Google doesn't?
a: eBay only searches its own listings, which it can push into Elasticsearch as JSON. Google searches the whole internet by crawling other people's servers, which Elasticsearch isn't designed for.

q: What is AWS OpenSearch?
a: AWS's fork of Elasticsearch, made after Elastic changed its license. The managed service also does vector search, so it's often the vector database in RAG pipelines.

q: What does each part of the ELK stack do?
a: Elasticsearch stores and searches the data, Logstash collects and transforms it on the way in, and Kibana is the web interface for searching and building dashboards. Beats are small agents that ship data from servers.

q: Does Logstash store data?
a: No. It's the pipeline in front of Elasticsearch: it reads input, parses and transforms it, for example with grok, and outputs it to Elasticsearch, which does the storing.

q: What language is the ELK stack written in?
a: Mixed. Elasticsearch and Logstash run on Java, Kibana is JavaScript, and Beats are written in Go.

q: What is a stakeholder?
a: Anyone in the company with a job-related interest in your project who isn't on the tech team, like the head of marketing for a marketing data project.

q: What does QA do on a data engineering team?
a: Reviews pull requests and tests them, usually in the UAT environment, to see if the change breaks the pipeline. If it does, they reject it with a note so the author can fix it.

q: How do you write an integration test for a data pipeline?
a: Create a small test dataset with known, deliberate flaws, send it through every stage of the pipeline, and check that each stage did what it should, using the same framework as unit tests, like PyTest.

q: What is code coverage?
a: The percentage of lines of code that have tests. It's usually checked automatically in CI/CD, for example with SonarQube.

q: What does the day-to-day work on a data migration look like?
a: Validating schemas and data types, tracking down columns that live somewhere else in the new system, and proving the data in the destination matches the source.

q: Why does governance matter more in a migration?
a: The old system's roles, permissions and masking rules have to be recreated in the new one, or data ends up exposed or inaccessible.

q: Which interview round usually decides the job?
a: The technical round where someone asks about your last project: what you built, what broke and how you fixed it. Memorized quiz answers don't get you through it, real experience does.

q: What are the three names for Databricks' declarative pipelines?
a: Lakeflow, Spark Declarative Pipelines and Delta Live Tables.

q: What is Auto Loader?
a: Databricks' incremental loading feature. Using cloudFiles as the readStream format, it only picks up new files since the last run and tracks what it has processed, with Lakeflow managing the checkpoints.

q: What is a Python decorator?
a: Something that adds functionality to a function without changing its existing behavior, written with an @ on the line above the def. In Lakeflow, decorators turn functions into tables, views and data-quality rules.

q: What's the difference between expect and expect_or_drop?
a: expect_or_drop removes rows that fail the condition. expect keeps the rows and only records the violations.

q: What's the difference between a view and a materialized view?
a: A view is a saved query that stores no data and re-runs every time you read it. A materialized view stores its results and is only updated when it's refreshed.

q: Silver failed saying Bronze couldn't be resolved. Where do you look?
a: At the first error. Silver's failure was a symptom of Bronze failing first, so you fix the Bronze traceback.

q: Why did the class need an explicit StructType schema?
a: Auto Loader inferred the nested data field as a string, so stations couldn't be exploded. An explicit schema with StructType and StructField told Spark the real nested structure.

q: What's the difference between Lakeflow and dbt?
a: Lakeflow, or DLT, only runs on Databricks and uses Python decorators or SQL with expectations. dbt works on many warehouses, especially Snowflake, and uses SQL models with YAML and dbt tests.

q: What is Delta MERGE?
a: An upsert. It matches source rows to target rows on a key, then updates, inserts or deletes them, all in one atomic commit.

q: What can make a MERGE fail?
a: The source having more than one row for the same key, which gives a "multiple source rows matched" error. Deduplicate the source first, for example with ROW_NUMBER.

q: What is time travel?
a: Querying a table as it looked at an earlier version or timestamp, with VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF. It works because the transaction log keeps every version. Delta, Iceberg and Hudi all support it.

q: How far back can Delta time travel go?
a: As long as the log and data files exist. By default history is kept 30 days and old files 7 days after VACUUM, and both are configurable. Snowflake's maximum is 90 days.

q: What does RESTORE do?
a: It rolls a table back to an earlier version by writing a new commit that points to the old files. The restore shows up in the history, so nothing is erased.

q: What's the difference between RESTORE, MERGE and VACUUM?
a: RESTORE rolls back to an old version, MERGE upserts new data, and VACUUM physically deletes old unreferenced files, which limits how far back you can time travel.

q: Is time travel the same as the LAG function?
a: No. LAG is a read-only window function comparing rows within one version of the data. Time travel compares whole versions of the table at different points in time.

q: How would you use time travel to find when bad records started?
a: Query older and older versions until you find one without the bad records, then use that version's timestamp from DESCRIBE HISTORY to see when the problem began.

q: What is idempotency?
a: An operation is idempotent if running it once or many times gives the same end result, with no duplicates. Pipelines need it because jobs get rerun.

q: Give examples of idempotent and non-idempotent writes.
a: A MERGE on a key, a partition overwrite and a checkpointed stream are idempotent. A plain INSERT or append with no key check, or count equals count plus one, are not.

q: What is CDC?
a: Change Data Capture: recording every insert, update and delete from a source as it happens. It's used for migrating tables that are still being written to and for keeping a lake or warehouse in sync with an operational database.

q: What's the best way to do CDC?
a: Log-based: read the database's transaction log, like the MySQL binlog or Postgres WAL, with a tool like Debezium or AWS DMS. Timestamp polling is simpler but misses hard deletes.

q: What's the difference between CDC and SCD?
a: CDC captures changes from a source as they happen, in seconds or minutes. SCD stores the long-term history of dimension attributes in the warehouse. CDC often feeds an SCD Type 2 merge.

q: What is SCD Type 2?
a: Each change closes the old row, setting valid_to and is_current false, and inserts a new current row. That keeps the full history, like every address a customer has had.

q: What are SCD Types 0, 1 and 3?
a: Type 0 never changes the original value, Type 1 overwrites it with no history, and Type 3 adds a column holding the previous value.

q: What problem does Auto Loader solve?
a: Incremental file ingestion. It picks up only new files in a folder, tracks which ones it loaded in a checkpoint, and handles schema inference and evolution, so you don't reread or duplicate files.

q: How do you use Auto Loader?
a: readStream with format cloudFiles and the option cloudFiles.format set to the file type, like json. Then writeStream to a Delta table with a checkpoint location.

q: What does trigger availableNow do?
a: It processes all the new data available, commits its progress and stops. It's the common choice for incremental batches run on a schedule.

q: Why are checkpoints important?
a: They record what was processed, so after a crash or restart the stream resumes from the last committed batch with nothing lost and nothing loaded twice. With a Delta sink that's exactly-once.

q: What's the difference between checkpointing and deduplication?
a: Checkpointing stops the same file or offset from being processed twice. Deduplication stops the same record from appearing twice, for example if it arrives in two different files.

q: What happens if you delete an Auto Loader checkpoint?
a: Auto Loader forgets what it loaded and reloads every file, which creates duplicates.

q: How does Auto Loader handle a new column?
a: In the default addNewColumns mode the stream stops once, records the new schema and works after a restart. Data that doesn't fit goes into the _rescued_data column.

q: What is a Lakeflow Job?
a: Databricks' built-in orchestrator. It runs tasks like notebooks, pipelines, SQL or dbt in a DAG with dependencies, schedules, retries and alerts.

q: What happens to downstream tasks when an upstream task fails?
a: With the default "All succeeded" setting they don't run and are marked upstream failed. You fix the problem and use a repair run to rerun only the failed tasks.

q: Why might a failed task succeed on retry?
a: If the failure was transient, like a network timeout, API throttling, a capacity issue or a file still being written. A code bug or bad data will fail again.

q: What's the difference between a Lakeflow Job and an ETL pipeline?
a: A Job is an orchestrator that runs any tasks in the order you set. An ETL pipeline, or DLT, is a declarative framework where you define tables and the engine works out the order, with expectations and automatic checkpoints.

q: Are Databricks Jobs part of ADF?
a: No. They're two separate schedulers. Jobs run inside Databricks, while ADF orchestrates many Azure services and can call Databricks.

q: Is ETL outdated?
a: No. ELT is preferred for lakehouses and cloud warehouses, but ETL still fits simpler targets like Postgres and pipelines that already work.

q: What is MLflow?
a: An open-source platform for the machine learning lifecycle, created by Databricks. It tracks experiments and runs, packages models, keeps a versioned model registry and helps serve models.

q: What's the difference between an experiment and a run?
a: An experiment groups attempts at one problem. A run is one training attempt with its own parameters, metrics and artifacts.

q: What's the difference between a param, a metric and an artifact?
a: A param is an input setting you chose, like max depth. A metric is a measured result, like MAE. An artifact is a saved file, like the model itself or a plot.

q: What are MLflow traces?
a: Step-by-step records of an LLM or agent app: each model call's input and output, tool calls, retrieval, timings and errors. They help you debug why the app answered the way it did.

q: What is tabular ML?
a: Traditional machine learning on rows and columns, like regression, random forests and gradient boosting, predicting a number or a class. It's different from LLMs, which generate text.

q: What's the difference between MAE and RMSE?
a: MAE is the average size of the error in the target's units, like off by 10 bikes. RMSE squares the errors first, so it punishes big misses more and is always at least as large as MAE.

q: What does toPandas do, and what's the risk?
a: It converts a Spark DataFrame to a pandas DataFrame, pulling all the rows into the driver's memory. On big data that can crash the driver, so limit or sample first.

q: What's a data engineer's role in MLOps?
a: Building the data pipelines and features, preparing training data, and deploying and running the infrastructure. Data scientists build the model itself.

q: How does a fraud-detection pipeline work?
a: Transactions stream in through Kafka or Event Hubs, features are computed, and a served model flags each one as OK or suspicious in real time. Flagged ones notify the customer. Model training on historical data runs in batch.

q: How do you choose an analytics platform?
a: Start from what the business needs, the data size, the budget and the infrastructure you already have. The best platform isn't the most functional or the cheapest, it's the one that gives the business what it needs the way it needs it.

q: What is a VPS?
a: A virtual private server: a computer in the cloud, like an EC2 instance, from any provider.

q: What is MinIO?
a: Object storage you host yourself that speaks the S3 API, so tools that read S3 can read it by changing the endpoint. With Iceberg it replaces the older HDFS and Hive setup.

q: What is DuckDB?
a: An in-process OLAP SQL engine, a library or single binary with no server. It's columnar and very fast on one machine and can query Parquet, CSV and JSON files directly.

q: Why does Iceberg need a catalog?
a: Every write creates a new metadata file, so something has to hold the single answer to which metadata file is current for each table and make commits atomic. That's the catalog, like Lakekeeper, Glue or Unity.

q: What is Azure Synapse?
a: Azure's analytics workspace and basically its equivalent of Redshift, combining serverless and dedicated SQL pools, Spark pools and pipelines in one studio.

q: What's the difference between a serverless and a dedicated SQL pool?
a: The serverless pool queries files in ADLS in place, needs no provisioning and bills per terabyte processed. The dedicated pool is a provisioned MPP warehouse that bills per hour while running, even idle, so you have to pause it.

q: How is Synapse serverless billed?
a: By data processed, not stored. A 1 GB dataset queried a thousand times counts as about a terabyte processed.

q: How do you keep serverless query costs down?
a: Query Parquet, select only the columns you need, filter on partitions, keep smaller aggregated tables with CETAS, and set a processing limit.

q: Define MPP.
a: Massively parallel processing, a shared-nothing architecture. Data is spread across many nodes, each with its own CPU, memory and storage. A leader splits the query, every node works on its slice in parallel, and the leader combines the results. Redshift, Snowflake, Synapse and Databricks all use it.

q: Why is it bad to keep data in one region and the warehouse in another?
a: Every query moves data a long way, which is slow and incurs data transfer charges. And crossing borders raises data residency issues under laws like GDPR.

q: What are GDPR, CCPA and LGPD?
a: Data privacy laws: GDPR in the EU, CCPA and CPRA in California, and LGPD in Brazil. They govern how and where personal data is stored and handled.

q: Why did the Synapse workspace fail to deploy in East US?
a: The region wasn't accepting new Azure SQL servers for that subscription, a capacity or quota restriction. Deploying in another region fixed it.

q: Why did queries fail with an error about the master database?
a: Serverless pools start in the master system database, where you can't create your own objects. You create a database and USE it first.

q: Can Synapse serverless read JSON?
a: Not with a JSON format option. You can read each file as one text column and parse it with OPENJSON, but the better answer is to flatten it once into Silver Parquet.

q: Why convert JSON to Parquet before querying with SQL?
a: SQL engines need flat, typed columns at one level. Parquet is structured, columnar and compressed, so queries are simpler, faster and cheaper.

q: Why use coalesce(4) when writing Silver?
a: To write a few medium files instead of many tiny ones, which avoids the small files problem and speeds up Synapse queries.

q: Does a view in Synapse serverless disappear when you log out?
a: No, it's saved in the database. But it stores no data, so every query re-scans the files and is billed again.

q: How do you persist query results in Synapse serverless?
a: With CETAS, create external table as select, which writes the results as new Parquet files. Materialized views only exist in dedicated pools.

q: How do you point a Kafka producer at Event Hubs?
a: Change the configuration, not the code: bootstrap servers to the namespace on port 9093, SASL_SSL with PLAIN, the username literally $ConnectionString, and the connection string as the password, kept as a secret.

q: The network-total query showed one snapshot with only one station. What should a pipeline do about that?
a: Add a completeness check in Gold that flags any snapshot with far fewer stations than normal, since it points to a partial file or bad timestamp.

q: What is Microsoft Fabric?
a: Microsoft's all-in-one SaaS analytics platform. It packages Data Factory, Spark notebooks, warehousing, real-time analytics and Power BI into one UI, on top of one shared storage layer called OneLake.

q: What's the main difference between Fabric and plain Azure?
a: OneLake. The compute services are basically the same Azure ones; Fabric bundles them in one interface on shared storage, while in Azure each service is separate and you wire them together.

q: Explain the layers under OneLake.
a: Blob Storage is flat object storage. ADLS Gen2 adds a hierarchical namespace. OneLake sits on ADLS and adds a tenant-wide unified namespace, a catalog and governance.

q: What does unified namespace mean?
a: You can work with data from many buckets and workspaces as one environment, instead of managing each storage account separately.

q: When is a unified platform like OneLake worth it?
a: For large organizations with many teams and very varied sources. For a small project or business, plain storage and a Spark or DuckDB engine is enough.

q: What is a Fabric capacity?
a: The pool of paid compute that all Fabric workloads run on. It's expensive, around eighty-four hundred dollars a month for the size shown, so you pause it or use a trial.

q: What is a schema registry for?
a: Storing every version of a stream's message schema, so consumers can apply the right schema to each message and schema changes can be checked for compatibility.

q: Can you mention Snowflake in a Fabric project story?
a: Not as part of the same pipeline. Fabric is all-in-one, so processing, storage and BI should all be in Fabric. External sources feeding it are fine.

q: How is TOP different from LIMIT?
a: They do the same thing. TOP is the Microsoft T-SQL dialect, used in SQL Server, Azure SQL and Synapse; LIMIT is used in Postgres, MySQL, Spark SQL and others, and doesn't work in T-SQL.

q: How do you count rows matching a condition next to the total?
a: Use COUNT star for the total and SUM of CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END for the matching rows.

q: What's the real difference between ADLS Gen2 and S3?
a: ADLS Gen2 has a hierarchical namespace with real directories, so folder renames are atomic and you can set ACLs on folders. S3 is flat, and its folders are just key prefixes.

q: How many sources can a Fabric copy job have?
a: One. You create a separate copy job for each source.

q: Where does a copy job put relational data versus files in a lakehouse?
a: Relational data goes into Tables as Delta tables; raw files go into the Files area, ideally a subfolder per source.

q: Why did the ADLS and S3 copy jobs fail?
a: Authentication. ADLS needed a valid key, SAS token or service principal, and the S3 connector rejected the s3 URI and wanted the HTTPS bucket URL plus working IAM keys.

q: What does the discharge-date filter in silver do?
a: It keeps rows where the patient hasn't been discharged yet or the discharge is on or after admission, and drops impossible rows where discharge comes before admission.

q: How do you compute a 30-day readmission?
a: Use a window partitioned by patient and ordered by admit date, use lag to get the previous discharge date, take the days between that and the new admission, and flag it if it's 30 or less.

q: What is a semantic model?
a: Power BI's data model: tables, relationships and measures that reports are built on. In Fabric you create one from the lakehouse's gold tables.

q: What are common Fabric interview questions?
a: Mostly "do you have Fabric experience?", which leads into your profile narrative. Be ready to tell the story: sources, Data Factory into OneLake, Spark notebooks bronze to gold, Power BI on Direct Lake.

q: How do you turn a non-data job into a data-engineering narrative?
a: Find the data the real system produced, like charging-station telemetry, and build a coherent pipeline around it: a stream like Kinesis, Spark Structured Streaming, a Delta bronze layer and a business use case like predictive maintenance.

q: What is Direct Lake?
a: A Power BI storage mode in Fabric where the semantic model reads the Delta files in OneLake directly, so you get near Import-mode speed without copying data or running live SQL queries.

q: Compare Import, DirectQuery and Direct Lake.
a: Import copies data into the model and needs refreshes, but it's fast. DirectQuery sends live queries to the source, which is fresh but slower. Direct Lake reads OneLake files directly, so it's fast and fresh, but only in Fabric.

q: What is DAX?
a: Power BI's formula language for measures and calculated columns. It looks a bit like SQL aggregations with pandas-style table and column references.

q: What is a measure?
a: A named calculation evaluated at query time for whatever filters a visual applies, so the same measure gives a total on a card and per-category values in a chart.

q: Why use DIVIDE instead of the slash operator?
a: DIVIDE handles division by zero by returning an alternate value you choose, like zero, instead of an error.

q: What is mirroring in Fabric?
a: Continuous replication of an operational database, like Azure SQL, into OneLake as Delta tables using change data capture, so the data is always available in Fabric without building pipelines.

q: Why did mirroring fail in class?
a: The SQL server and Fabric were in different tenants, and mirroring with a managed identity can't cross tenants. It's an architectural restriction, not a missing permission.

q: What is a managed identity?
a: An identity Azure creates and manages for a resource so it can authenticate to other services without stored passwords. A system-assigned one lives and dies with the resource.

q: Map Event Hubs terms to Kafka.
a: A namespace is like a Kafka cluster, an event hub is like a topic, and both have partitions and consumer groups.

q: Why create separate Send and Listen policies?
a: Least privilege. The producer can only send and the consumer can only read, so a leaked key does less damage.

q: Why did the consumer print a burst of events first?
a: Event Hubs retained the events sent before the consumer started. A new consumer reading from the beginning processes that backlog first, then new events as they arrive, just like Kafka.

q: When does a while True loop stop?
a: Only when it's stopped manually or by an external failure. For streaming that's desirable, because data can arrive at any time.

q: What is a graceful shutdown?
a: Stopping a producer or consumer cleanly: catching Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, flushing buffered messages, closing the client and committing offsets, so nothing is lost or reprocessed.

q: What is a Fabric Eventstream?
a: A no-code Fabric item that ingests a stream from a source like Event Hubs and routes it to destinations like an Eventhouse or a lakehouse.

q: What is an Eventhouse?
a: Fabric's real-time analytics store, based on Azure Data Explorer. It holds KQL databases optimized for time-series event data.

q: What is KQL?
a: Kusto Query Language, a read-only language where you start with a table and pipe rows through operators like where, summarize, order by and render.

q: Why send the same stream to both an Eventhouse and a lakehouse?
a: It's the hot and cold path pattern. The Eventhouse gives live dashboards in seconds, and the lakehouse bronze table feeds the medallion pipeline for joined, historical analytics.

q: A Fabric notebook says no default context exists. What do you do?
a: Attach the lakehouse in the Explorer and set it as the default lakehouse, so table names resolve.

q: What does net admissions mean in the gold table?
a: Admissions minus discharges, roughly how many patients are currently admitted.

q: What did Evan say is the real difference between all these platforms?
a: Not much. It's the same process dressed up differently: Kafka, Kinesis, Event Hubs and Pub/Sub all stream, and notebooks are notebooks. The differences are specific features like Direct Lake and mirroring.

q: How do you stop bad data from spreading?
a: Validate between bronze and silver with not-null, range and duplicate checks, quarantine failures, use data quality gates that stop the pipeline, and alert on them.

q: When are the capstone presentations?
a: A practice run on Monday, November 2, and the real presentations on Friday, November 6.

q: What does the capstone need at minimum?
a: An ingestion job into cloud object storage, processing up through bronze, silver and gold, and a visualization connected to the gold data, ideally with a tool other than Databricks' built-in charts. It doesn't have to be multi-cloud.

q: How is GCP different from AWS and Azure?
a: Mostly it isn't. It's the same set of services with a few Google conveniences, like easy sign-up with a Google account, a friendlier storage console, and one-click permission buttons.

q: What is Cloud Dataflow?
a: GCP's fully managed, autoscaling data processing service that runs Apache Beam pipelines, batch or streaming. It fills the same role as Glue or a Databricks notebook.

q: What is Apache Beam?
a: A unified programming model for batch and streaming. It has no engine of its own. You write the pipeline once and choose a runner, like the direct runner locally or the Dataflow runner on GCP.

q: What does the pipe symbol mean in Beam code?
a: It applies the next transform to the data from the previous step, so each line is one step of the pipeline. The label before the double arrow names the step.

q: What's the difference between map and flatMap?
a: Map gives exactly one output per input. FlatMap can give zero or many and flattens nested collections, so a list of lists becomes one flat list.

q: What is Dataproc?
a: GCP's managed Spark and Hadoop service. Its serverless Spark option is like EMR Serverless.

q: What made BigQuery special when it launched?
a: It was the first serverless data warehouse. There's no cluster to provision, storage is cheap, and you pay mainly for the data your queries scan.

q: How do you reduce BigQuery costs?
a: Select only the columns you need, partition and cluster tables so filters skip data, and check the bytes estimate before running. LIMIT doesn't reduce the bytes scanned.

q: What's the GCP equivalent of Lambda, ECS, MWAA and RDS?
a: Cloud Run functions, Cloud Run, Cloud Composer and Cloud SQL.

q: What's the difference between AWS DMS and GCP Storage Transfer Service?
a: DMS is database-aware: it connects to a database and replicates tables. STS moves files and objects between storage systems into Cloud Storage, so it can't read straight from Postgres.

q: Which tool would migrate S3 or Hadoop files into GCP?
a: Storage Transfer Service. For scheduled loads into BigQuery there's also the BigQuery Data Transfer Service.

q: Should a migration transform the data?
a: No. A migration makes a complete, unmodified copy with the same schema and row count. You transform afterwards in a separate step.

q: Why did the new GCP project's billing never enable?
a: Billing on new projects was blocked by a quota, and raising it takes a request and about two days. The fix was to use an existing project that already had billing.

q: How does Storage Transfer Service get access to an S3 bucket without access keys?
a: You create an AWS IAM role that trusts Google's transfer service account through web identity federation, and give that role read access to the whole path you're copying.

q: What does ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE do in Postgres?
a: It's an upsert. If the key already exists, it updates the row instead of inserting a duplicate, and EXCLUDED refers to the values you tried to insert.

q: How should you describe Spark and Kafka in an AWS project narrative?
a: Say PySpark running on EMR Serverless or Glue, and Amazon MSK for Kafka. Plain Spark and Kafka suggest an on-prem setup.

q: When does it make sense to use Databricks and Snowflake in the same project?
a: Only when another team, business unit or partner company uses Snowflake and your Databricks team has to work with them. Otherwise Databricks can do the reporting itself.

q: Should you say bronze, silver, gold or raw, curated, semantic?
a: Bronze, silver and gold. They're the most common terms, and first-round interviewers often work from a checklist that uses them.

q: When are the practice run and the final presentations?
a: The practice run is Monday, November 2, and the final presentations are Friday, November 6.

q: How should a data app feed fresh pipeline data to an AI model?
a: Usually by running a SQL query and putting the results in the prompt. RAG with a vector database is only worth it when you need to keep querying a body of unstructured content.

q: Which service account do Dataflow workers run as, and what roles does it need?
a: The project's default Compute Engine service account. It needs the Dataflow worker role, storage object admin for the buckets, and BigQuery data editor and job user roles if it writes to BigQuery.

q: How do you run the same Beam script locally and on Dataflow?
a: Change the runner flag. DirectRunner runs it on your machine; DataflowRunner submits it to GCP along with project, region, temp and staging locations and worker settings.

q: Why test with the DirectRunner first?
a: It runs on your laptop, so bugs cost nothing, and a Dataflow job takes minutes just to start workers.

q: What does parse_known_args do in a Beam script?
a: It separates the options you defined, like input and output, from everything else, which gets passed to Beam as pipeline options like runner and project.

q: Is Beam an execution engine?
a: No. Beam is the programming model and SDK. A runner like Dataflow, Spark or Flink actually executes the pipeline.

q: What's the common shape of a pipeline on every cloud?
a: Ingest into object storage, process the data up through bronze, silver and gold, load gold into a warehouse, and connect BI or AI tools on top.

q: Why add a key and then remove it in a Beam pipeline?
a: Per-key transforms like CombinePerKey need key-value pairs. You key by something like station ID, combine to keep the newest record per station, then drop the key with Values before writing.

q: Why did the silver-to-gold job fail with "missing 1 required positional argument b"?
a: The combine function took two arguments, but CombinePerKey with a plain function passes it one iterable of values. Rewriting it to take the iterable and return the newest record fixed it.

q: What do CREATE_NEVER and WRITE_TRUNCATE mean in WriteToBigQuery?
a: CREATE_NEVER means the table must already exist. WRITE_TRUNCATE replaces the table's contents on each run, so reruns don't duplicate data.

q: Does each step in Beam code show up in the Dataflow graph?
a: Yes, each labeled step is a box in the job graph, which is a directed acyclic graph. Dataflow may fuse steps internally, but the labels help with monitoring and debugging.

q: Should one pipeline write to both a warehouse and a NoSQL store?
a: Usually build two dedicated pipelines. If one target is decommissioned, you just turn off its schedule instead of changing and redeploying shared code.

q: How do you get the latest row per key in BigQuery?
a: Use QUALIFY with ROW_NUMBER over a partition by the key ordered by timestamp descending, and keep row number one.

q: What does QUALIFY do?
a: It filters on the result of a window function, the way HAVING filters on aggregates.

q: How do you cut BigQuery table scan costs?
a: Partition by date, cluster by commonly filtered columns, and select only the columns you need.

q: The data showed a first snapshot in 1970. What does that mean?
a: Some timestamps were zero or missing and got converted to the Unix epoch. A silver or gold quality check should reject or null those.

q: How do you connect Looker Studio to BigQuery?
a: Create a blank report, add data, pick the BigQuery connector, then choose the project, dataset and table or view.

q: How did the bubble map finally work in Looker Studio?
a: By making a text field of latitude comma longitude in a BigQuery view, refreshing the data source's fields, setting that field's type to geo latitude-longitude, and recreating the chart.

q: Is building a loan risk-scoring algorithm a data engineer's job?
a: No. That belongs to data scientists, finance and application developers. The data engineer makes the input data available and lands the decisions in the stream and the warehouse for analytics and compliance.

q: How much should you know about a company's internal data tools?
a: What they are and what they do. Beyond that, it's reasonable to say you ingested data from them and treated them as a black box.
